pr_title: tmpfiles: extend "Age" to accept an "age-by" argument
pr_body:
For `systemd-tmpfiles --cleanup`, if the `Age` parameter is specified, the criteria for deletion is determined from the path's last modification timestamp (`mtime`), its last access timestamp (`atime`) and the last status change timestamp (`ctime`).

For instance, if one of those paths to be cleaned up are opened, it results in the modification of `atime`, which results file system entry to not be removed because the default aging algorithm would skip the entry.

Add an optional `age-by` argument by extending the `Age` parameter to restrict the clean-up for a particular type of file timestamp, which can be specified in `tmpfiles.d` as follows:


```
  [age-by:]cleanup-age, where age-by is "[abcmABCM]+"
```

For example:
```
  d /foo/bar - - - abM:1m -
```

Would clean-up any files that were not accessed and created, or directories that were not modified less than a minute ago in `/foo/bar`.


Fixes: #17002
pr_comments:
Summary of changes since the last commit:

@poettering - Can you please review?

@poettering - Can you please take a look? Thanks!

Summary of changes:
 - added `AGE_BY_DEFAULT_DIR` and `AGE_BY_DEFAULT_FILE` using the same set of flags
 - cleaned up `parse_age_by_from_arg` (dropped repeating characters for `IN_SET`)
 - allow `C` to be passed as an argument for directories (but ignore it when checking timestamps)
 - updated the comments in `dir_cleanup()` about why `continue` is used (https://github.com/systemd/systemd/pull/19440#discussion_r625176387)

@poettering - Can you please review? Thanks.

> Yes. I would say specifying `amcb:1h` is not the same as `1h` (with `AGE_BY_DEFAULT_FILE`). In the former, we don't delete a file if at least one of the specified timestamp types is older than the cut-off time, whereas in the latter, we don't delete a file even if one of the timestamp types is newer than the cutoff time

Can you elaborate on the usecase why you want to focus on the oldest of the selected timestamps instead of the newest of the selected timestamps of the file?

If there's indeed a usecase for this it appears to me this should have a modifier of it's own to select this "inverted" behaviour. i.e. `am:1h` would mean "delete this if neither atime nor mtime have been updated in the last hour". and the additional syntax `~am:1h` or so would instead mean "delete this if either atime or mtime have been updated in the last hour". The latter is what you are after, right?

But still, I'd like to understnad the usecase for that logic. Can you elaborate?

> and the additional syntax ~am:1h or so would instead mean "delete this if either atime or mtime have been updated in the last hour". The latter is what you are after, right?

Correct. But I realize now, that it would not be necessary.

For example, let's say there's are files in the directory that is being written to frequently (and this keeps updating it's `mtime`, but it's `btime` will remain the same). If the age-by is set to `mb:15m` - we want to retain files that were created or modified 15 mins ago, and clean up the rest.

So, for the two options we have:
  - option 1: "delete files with `mtime` _and_ `btime` older than an hour" - would check the modify and create times, and let's say it was modified a minute ago. Since the `mtime` is newer, we wouldn't check the `btime` and the file will not be cleaned up. This makes sense.

  - option 2: "delete files with `mtime` _or_ `btime` older than an hour" - would check for modify and create times. But in this case, would also account for the older `btime`, and the file would get cleaned up. This should not happen, right?

Thinking a little bit about this, what you initially suggested ("option 1") makes sense - i.e., check for timestamps that were asked for, and don't delete a file if at least one of them is newer. If the user explicitly specifies something like `mb:15m`, they would want to retain files that were modified or created less than 15 minutes ago. So, if one of those timestamps is newer (say `mtime`), we should keep the file around. There is no need to check for the other timestamp (`btime`). So, checking for both the timestamps of a file is unnecessary here.

I can't think of a use-case that would warrant for "option 2". Shall I go ahead and make the following change, and update the PR?

> ```c
> if (age_by_dir & AGE_BY_MTIME) {
>	if (mtime_nsec != NSEC_INFINITY && mtime_nsec >= cutoff_nsec) {
>		/* Skip deletion; don't check for other times. */
>		continue;
>}
>
>/* Check for other timestamps. */
>```

Changes since the last commit:

  - updated tests for the change above

Also, `btime` isn't working because it might be set to 0. Please see https://github.com/systemd/systemd/pull/19440#discussion_r628371663 about why the tests are failing.

@poettering - Can you PTAL?

issue_context.title: tmpfiles.d possibility of aging by mtime without considering atime
issue_context.body:
I have some log directories with programs that generate some files (one such case is Mod Security with the parallel log, other is Tomcat 6 or before, with logs by day, etc.) which I think tmpfiles.d would be useful to use to delete the old log files.

The problem is that sometimes one needs to inspect some log file and then it changes it's atime which causes tmpfiles.d to not delete them.

Having some way to specify that the Age option looks into mtime only would be nice for such cases.

These are not good candidates for LogRotate.

So for example being able to say this:
`
e     /var/log/tomcat6/ -    -    -    31d mtime
`

review_comments:
hmm, actually, thinking about this, I think it would be a lot more natural, if we'd have AgeBy with just one set of the four values, and then use it twice in the Item structure. 

i.e. drop the _F and _D stuff here, so that there are only four bits defined. Then also add:

```
AGE_BY_DEFAULT_DIRECTORY = AGE_BY_ATIME|AGE_BY_BTIME|AGE_BY_MTIME,
AGE_BY_DEFAULT_FILE = AGE_BY_ATIME|AGE_BY_BTIME|AGE_BY_CTIME|AGE_BY_MTIME,
```
maybe drop the `if (seconds)` line and instead move the `a = seconds;` line into the `if (r >= 0)` block. After all, `seconds` will be set exactly when split_pair() was successful

hmm, why have AGE_BY_UNSET here?

i.e. i think our default behaviour should be something we encode here as AGE_BY_DEFAULT or so, which is just a combo of bits we define here.

Well, `AGE_BY_UNSET` reverts back to the default behavior in `dir_cleanup()`, where the loop `continue`s when a "too new" entry is found immediately instead of checking for the rest of the file timestamp types, and then checking for the masks. Isn't that faster?
I think I understand what you meant, dropped `AGE_BY_UNSET` for `AGE_BY_DEFAULT`.
So, `i` is used below to check for an invalid character.

then maybe move the declaration to the beginning of the block, i.e. right after the `for (…) {`

otherwise this is a bit confusing, given that you use it at various places but only define it close to one of them.
so is this a bit mask? or a regular enum? you seem to implement it mostly as regular one, but here you declare it as a mask?
Yes, it is an `enum`, but the shifts were added to see where the `1` would be set (like a flag). Are you suggesting that I change it `1, 2, 4, ...`?

no, the `1 << 0`, `1 << 1`, … is the right way to denote bit masks. I just found it confusing that you only allowed one of them to be specifying per tmpfiles.d line, even though it actually was a bitmask already, which suggests you allow combinations. And you *should* allow combinations
Oh, OK. Right, now that we want to allow multiple values to be set, we can keep it that way. :)
please propagate all errors here, except for EINVAL. i.e. when handling errors, there should always be a catchall for unexpected errors. it's only EINVAL that we need to take care of explicitly
